newsitem.title: USA: Sands unveils $2.0 bln Venetian hotel in Las Vegas.
newsitem.headline: Sands unveils $2.0 bln Venetian hotel in Las Vegas.

text.p: Management of the Sands Hotel in Las Vegas on Tuesday unveiled a $2.0 billion plan to build the world's largest hotel and casino themed around the Italian city of Venice.

The all-suite hotel, to be called "The Venetian", will be built on 40 acres formerly occupied by the privately-owned Sands that was razed about nine months ago. It will rely on traffic at nearby convention centers to fill its 6,000 rooms.
A ground breaking ceremony took place on Monday, and the first 3,000 rooms will be opened in Spring 1999 with the second 3,000 available the following year.

"We are going to have a five-star quality resort -- although it will be rather large -- but we'll have as quality a product as any in Las Vegas," Bill Weidner, chief operating officer, told Reuters in a phone interview.
As it is planned, the Venetian will feature classic Italian architecture, cobbled walkways and canals that wind through the property.

Two casinos each containing about 100,000 square feet of gambling space will be attached to the property's two towers that house the suites. Each suite will include a separate bedroom, sunken living room and marble-tiled bathroom.
When finished, the Venetian will eclipse in size the MGM Grand Hotel, owned by MGM Grand Inc, as the world's largest resort/casino, according to the Sands management.

MGM Grand opened in 1993 with over 5,000 rooms at a total cost of over $1.0 billion. Currently, Mirage Resorts Inc is building a hotel called "Bellagio" that will hold over 3,000 rooms and cost over $1.25 billion.
The rising supply of rooms in Las Vegas has concerned some gambling industry experts because it could lead to price competition among hotels, which could cut into profits.
In recent years, Las Vegas operators have relied on room revenue and 90-percent occupancy rates to spur earnings.

The effect of increasing supply can be seen in recent statistics from the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority. The room base totaled over 101,000 in January 1997 versus 90,000 in Jan. 1998, but total occupancy dipped to 84.5 percent from 87.3 percent.
The supply of rooms is expected to rise to over 114,000 by the end of 1998.

Like many operators, however, Weidner was little concerned by rising supply, noting that in the past 20 years, Las Vegas has been able to successfully boost the number of visitors to the city and absorb room supply.
